turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Helen. Have a seat and I'll grab your blood pressure and pulse before Dr Nguyen's free.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning. It'll be sky high, I can feel it already. Does one bad reading mean something's wrong, or do you need a whole pile of them?
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): The doctor will make sense of it, not me. Hold still... one hundred and fifty-two over ninety-four, and your pulse is seventy-six, nice and regular.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): One hundred and fifty-two over ninety-four? That's awful. Should I be worried right this second, like, do I need to lie down?
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): It's a bit up, but you're wound up, and Dr Nguyen will talk it through. Head on in, both of you.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thanks. She's been in a proper spin about this appointment all week, haven't you, Mum.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello Helen, I'm Dr Nguyen. Sorry to keep you waiting. And you've got someone with you?
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sarah, her daughter. I drove her over from her place this morning.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good on you for coming. Helen, what are we doing today?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): A check-up, that's all. Sarah made me book it. I feel fine, honestly. What do you actually do in a check-up, do you go looking for trouble?
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): We start with whatever you tell me, then I have a look, and we only test what seems worth it. Nurse has you at one fifty-two over ninety-four today. Any chest pain?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I'd hardly be sitting here nattering if I had chest pain.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. What about getting short of breath?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose... sometimes, not really. I can't give you a straight yes or no, sorry.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She stops halfway up the stairs at her place. Hand on the rail, just standing there. I've watched her do it heaps of times.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Those stairs are steep, Sarah. I'm sixty-six, not twenty. You're making a fuss.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): When you stop on those stairs, what do you feel in the chest? Is it pain, or something else?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I wouldn't call it pain. On the stairs it's a tight feeling, like a belt cinched round my chest. Is a tight feeling the same as pain, though? They reckon women don't get the proper sort.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tightness counts, even when it isn't a stab. Does it come on when you walk fast as well, or only on the stairs?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Walking fast too. It's been a couple of months — no, hang on, about three months. Hill by the shops, or if I'm legging it for the tram. If I slow down it eases off.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): See, she does know. She just keeps telling me it's nothing.

[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): So, about three months, tight across the chest on stairs or a fast walk, and it eases if you slow down. Thinking out loud, that pattern can be angina, the heart asking for more blood when you push it. It might just as easily be plain unfitness. I can't split those two on the story alone.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Angina? So it is my heart, then? Am I going to have a heart attack in the waiting room? My neighbour got a stent — do I need one of those?

[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not a heart attack today, and nobody's booking a stent from this chair. Angina is one possibility, not a label I'm sticking on you. Does the tightness ever show up when you're sitting still, say watching telly?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never when I'm sitting, only if I push myself, and if I stop it goes. That's a good sign, isn't it? Please tell me it is.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): It's a bit reassuring that rest settles it, yes, but it doesn't mean we park it. Any nausea when the tightness comes?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No nausea. Nothing like that.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): And sweating, getting clammy, along with it?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose... sometimes, not really. That hill makes me warm anyway. I couldn't swear to a clammy thing.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, I keep pelting you with questions. If I just ignore this, what's the worst that happens? I don't want to drop in the aisle at the shops.

[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): If exertional tightness is left alone long enough it can lead to a heart attack later, which is exactly why we don't wave it off. Nothing in front of me says that's on the cards this morning. Are you taking any tablets?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, a blood pressure one. Ramipril, five milligrams — no, sorry, I always muddle it, it's perindopril, eight milligrams. One in the morning, I swallow it with my cuppa.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Perindopril eight milligrams each morning, by mouth. Been on that a fair while for the blood pressure?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the high blood pressure. Years now. I don't miss that one. Is eight milligrams a huge dose, and could the tablet be what's making the chest go tight?

[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Eight is a perfectly ordinary dose, and perindopril doesn't usually give you effort tightness. The high blood pressure is what we've been treating, and one clinic reading doesn't make me change it today. Anything else in the box — aspirin, a statin?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Aspirin, yeah. The Cartia, a hundred milligrams. I'm meant to take it every day, but it's on and off, I forget. Is forgetting going to make me clot?
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She forgets more days than she remembers. I'll find the blister pack still full on a Friday.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): That's a bit harsh, Sarah. I do take it some days, I just can't promise it's every day. So does missing it matter or not?

[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Well, if it's hit and miss I can't pretend I know what you're actually getting, so the aspirin-taking stays a question mark. Don't swallow extras to catch up. Do keep the perindopril going every morning, same as now.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me have a listen to your heart and your lungs. Heart sounds are normal, there's no murmur, and your chest is clear. No swelling around the ankles.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Normal sounds — so it isn't the heart after all? Can you actually hear angina, or not? I need this in plain English.

[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): No, you can't hear angina with a stethoscope. A clear chest and normal heart sounds are good, but they don't cancel the tightness you've described. I'm still keeping possible angina on the list until the tests talk.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): My brain's gone to custard, sorry. Sarah, did you even see the cricket last night, or were you stuck getting Ollie down?
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Telly was on low. We batted like we'd never met a cricket ball. Ollie was supposed to be asleep and he kept creeping out for another look.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Five going on forty, that kid. Sunday he had me bowling underarm in the park and he wouldn't hear of the real rules.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Underarm in the park, that's how they all start. Did you get the sun, or was it tipping down?
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sun, thank goodness. Ice blocks after. He's already nominated the exact bat he wants for his birthday, the nerve.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't you buy the pricey one. His other nanna will cave, she always does. They're saying the weather turns this weekend, so the park's probably a write-off anyway.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): Rain all Saturday, apparently. Decent excuse for a cuppa on the couch instead of chasing a five-year-old round the boundary.
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll still want to go, mud and all. Mum, are you still right to have him Thursday arvo if it stays dry? Actually, don't answer that in here.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): We'll sort Thursday at home. Tell him Nanna says stay off the real pitch. I still can't get over that dropped catch at mid-off.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yeah, that was a shocker. Right, I'll drag us back to the plan, if that's alright.

[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): Here's what I want to do. An ECG before you leave, the nurse can do it in the side room, plus a pathology form for bloods — cholesterol, blood sugar, and kidney function because you're on the perindopril.

[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): ECG, that's the sticky dots, yeah? Does it hurt? And if the sugar comes back high, is that diabetes — I've never been told I've got diabetes. Can that tablet wreck your kidneys, is that why you're checking?

[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sticky dots, no pain, over in a few minutes. I can't see a diabetes diagnosis anywhere, and the sugar is just a check, not me deciding you've got it. Kidney bloods are routine when someone's on perindopril, not because I think yours are failing.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): And if the ECG looks bad, do I go to hospital from here? I haven't got a bag. Sarah, is the parking meter alright? Sorry, that's daft, I'm just rattled.
[SEG0057] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Meter's fine, Mum. Just hear the doctor out.

[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the tracing showed something urgent I'd deal with it before you walked out, but with a three-month story it's often normal and we still follow the symptoms. The bloods won't be back today. Come back next week and we'll sit down with all of it.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Next week. What am I allowed to do till then? Can I walk to the shops, and what if that belt thing starts in the aisle?

[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): Walk, but don't rush, and give that hill a miss for now. If the tightness comes on while you're resting, or it hasn't eased within a few minutes of stopping, ring an ambulance — don't have Sarah drive you. Anything else before I print this?
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the aspirin. Do I take it tonight, or leave it, seeing I've been so hopeless with it?

[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): Take today's dose if you haven't had it, the hundred milligrams, and aim for every day from here. No doubling up. Nurse will collect you for the ECG in a tick, and reception can book you back next week.
[SEG0063] person_1 (NURSE): I'll take you through for that ECG in the side room once you're wrapped up, Helen. It's quick.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. Thank you. Sorry about the twenty questions. Sarah, don't let me walk off without the form.
[SEG0065] person_4 (DOCTOR): The questions are why you came. We'll see you next week.

symptoms.name: tight feeling like a belt cinched round the chest
stops halfway up the stairs holding the rail
sweating or clamminess with the chest tightness

clinical_assessment.assessment: Exertional chest tightness could be angina or plain unfitness, and angina is only a possibility
clinical_assessment.basis: About three months of tightness across the chest on stairs or a fast walk that eases if she slows down; angina and unfitness cannot be split on the story alone

clinical_assessment.assessment: Possible angina remains on the list because a clear chest and normal heart sounds do not rule it out
clinical_assessment.normalized_assessment: Possible angina not excluded by examination
clinical_assessment.basis: Normal heart sounds and a clear chest do not cancel the described tightness

clinical_actions.description: ECG
Cholesterol blood test
Blood sugar
Kidney function blood test
Keep taking perindopril every morning as at present
One clinic blood pressure reading does not lead to changing blood pressure treatment today
Take aspirin 100 mg today if not already taken and then every day, without doubling up missed doses
Walk but do not rush, and avoid the hill for now
Ring an ambulance if chest tightness occurs at rest or does not ease within a few minutes of stopping, and do not be driven there
If the ECG shows something urgent, deal with it before she leaves; with a three-month history the ECG is often normal and the symptoms still need follow-up
Follow-up consultation

spec.situation: Man or woman 50-70 who comes 'for a check-up' and only slowly admits a tight feeling in the chest when climbing stairs or walking fast; first denies chest pain, later describes the tightness. Takes a BP tablet and aspirin on and off. Doctor orders ECG and bloods.
features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

bad.reason: No diabetes diagnosis is stated by doctor; not clearly reported by patient as absent past condition.
Aspirin 100 mg daily is intended, but current use is inconsistent/on-and-off, not clearly currently used daily.
bad.text: aspirin (dose=100 mg, frequency=once daily, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Exertional chest tightness is specifically described as 'like a belt cinched round my chest' and occurs only with exertion, not as pain/stabbing pain.
Shortness of breath was asked about and the patient gave an equivocal answer ('sometimes, not really'); daughter reports she stops halfway up the stairs holding the rail.
Chest pain was specifically denied when asked ('No. No chest pain.').
Sweating/clamminess with the tightness was asked about and the answer was uncertain/equivocal rather than absent or present ('sometimes, not really... couldn't swear to a clammy thing').
Doctor advised that one clinic blood pressure reading does not lead to changing her blood pressure treatment today.

Aspirin recording is inaccurate as fully current once-daily use: patient said Cartia 100 mg is prescribed daily but she takes it inconsistently/on and off and often forgets; daughter says she forgets more days than remembers.
Doctor stated that possible angina remains on the list despite normal examination and that normal heart sounds/clear chest do not rule it out.
Doctor stated that if the ECG showed something urgent, it would be dealt with before she left; with a three-month history the ECG is often normal and symptoms still need follow-up.
